title: IDLM: Inverse-distilled Diffusion Language Models
claim: Standard training fits a slow model from data; inverse distillation fixes the trained model and learns a fast generator.
layout: 3 stacked bands, top and bottom banners, central bidirectional arrows between distribution and model
description: The figure has three horizontal bands. The top purple-bordered banner covers standard Diffusion Language Models. It says 'Given: target distribution p*(x0)' and 'Train: diffusion model f*', with f* = argmin L(f, p*). It carries a green check for good quality and a red cross for slow inference. The middle band has a yellow histogram on the left for the data distribution. On the right is a transformer-style block, a blue bar with grey input boxes below and white output boxes above. Between them are a red right-pointing arrow and a left-pointing arrow, with a pink box reading 'From what we are given to what we train'. The bottom purple banner covers Inverse-distilled DLMs. The roles are swapped: 'Train: distribution p_θ' and 'Given: pretrained f*', with f* = argmin L(f, p_θ). It shows two green checks, for good quality and fast inference. Blue marks 'given' and green marks 'train'.
caption: Diffusion training vs inverse distillation. DLMs learn a slow teacher $f^*$ from data. IDLM fixes $f^*$ and learns $p_\theta$ for fast few-step generation.
abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently achieved strong results in text generation. However, their multi-step sampling leads to slow inference, limiting practical use. To address this, we extend Inverse Distillation, a technique originally developed to accelerate continuous diffusion models, to the discrete setting. Nonetheless, this extension introduces both theoretical and practical challenges. From a theoretical perspective, the inverse distillation objective lacks uniqueness guarantees, which may lead to suboptimal solutions. From a practical standpoint, backpropagation in the discrete space is non-trivial and often unstable. To overcome these challenges, we first provide a theoretical result demonstrating that our inverse formulation admits a unique solution, thereby ensuring valid optimization. We then introduce gradient-stable relaxations to support effective training. As a result, experiments on multiple DLMs show that our method, Inverse-distilled Diffusion Language Models (IDLM), reduces the number of inference steps by 4x-64x, while preserving the teacher model's generation quality. We provide the code, model checkpoints, and video tutorials on the project page: https://david-cripto.github.io/idlm-project-page
